Learn about other national symbols. History of the American flag The flag of the United States is a symbol of freedom before which Americans recite the pledge of allegiance . The flag's 13 red and white stripes represent the 13 original colonies. Its 50 white stars on a blue background represent the 50 states. Each of the colors on the flag has a meaning: Red: valor and bravery White: purity and innocence Blue: vigilance, perseverance, and justice A star is added to the flag when a new state joins the United States. The flag was last modified on July 4, 1960, when Hawaii was incorporated as a state. Learn more about the evolution of the American flag and its earlier designs. How to raise the flag Follow these guidelines to properly display the American flag [PDF, 162KB]. When to fly the flag at half-staff The American flag flies at half-staff or at half-mast when the country or a state is in mourning. The president, a state governor, or the mayor of the District of Columbia can order flags to fly at half-staff. PETER BREUNIG By Carlos Micó Published July 27, 2026 In 1886, when Nigeria was a colony of the British Empire, the Royal Niger Company gained exclusive mineral rights over the Jos Plateau in central Nigeria, an area rich in tin ore and inhabited by the Berom people. In the foothills, access routes to the mines ran through an area called Nok. Over the years, with the exploitation of the mines and the local people who overwhelmingly provided the labor force, numerous fragments of ancient pottery came to light but were largely ignored. One piece, too striking to be disregarded, appeared in 1928: a small monkey head, sculpted in terra-cotta. The mine manager, Lt. Col. John Dent Young, had that piece and other fragments transferred to a museum in the city of Jos, the provincial capital. Fifteen years later, a miner found another terra-cotta head and took it home, where he used it as a scarecrow, apparently with some success. Enheduanna is often identified as the first author who appears independently in the historical record. Her hymns to the gods of Akkad and Sumer survived centuries after her death—and their translations are changing what modern scholars know about the role of women in the ancient Middle East. Photo Illustration, NGM Staff. Source Photo for Illustration: Yale Peabody Museum By Liddy Berman Published September 8, 2026 More than 4,000 years ago, Enheduanna, high priestess of the Sumerian moon god and daughter of a king, labored over a palm-size clay tablet. Reed stylus in her hand, she pressed its tiny wedge-shaped tip into the clay to build the small, spiky characters of cuneiform. She had been driven from her temple home by a rebel leader who opposed her family’s imperial rule over the kingdoms of Ur and Uruk. Though exiled and frightened, she was far from powerless—her words were believed to influence the gods. In her writings, Enheduanna petitioned her patron goddess— Inanna , the Mesopotamian deity of love, war and change—to rescue her from the dark fate awaiting political exiles and restore her to her rightful position as high priestess. A new discovery reveals how close they came to finding an empire-altering fortune. Roman money, like this coin bearing the profile of Emperor Claudius, often contained silver, one of several precious metals that fueled Rome. Photograph by Robert Kawka, Alamy Stock Photo By Julian Sancton Art by Aria Safarzadegan Published July 21, 2025 The passage is easy to miss. A paragraph-long anecdote in the Annals by the Roman historian Tacitus, it tells a story found nowhere else, about an unpopular legate forcing legionaries into a treacherous mine at the frontier of the empire. It takes place during the reign of Claudius (A.D. 41–54), a time of furious expansion when Rome sought to swallow up the borderlands and their resources. The location mentioned in the Tacitus passage is vague, described as “in the district of Mattium,” just outside of Roman-occupied Germania Superior . But the goal is clear: to find more of a metal that powered the realm. ( Female Gladiators? pages.text: The Artisans Trying to Bring Back Neolithic Fashion | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The Artisans Trying to Bring Back Neolithic Fashion A growing community of craftspeople are trying to build knowledge of ancient clothing—by making it themselves. Historical craft specialist Vasi Birchwood recreates fashion from the Neolithic period on her Youtube channel. This outfit is one of her creations. The jacket is made of deer skin, stitched with deer skin cord and a bone awl, and adorned with moose teeth. The shirt underneath the jacket is made of undyed linen, hand stitched with linen thread. The skirt is made of deer skin and decorated with braided hemp strings. Photo Illustration: NGM Staff; Source Photos for Illustration: Vasi Birchwood By Starre Vartan Published November 2, 2026 Around the fire, no one seems especially bothered by the rain. Some people duck beneath bark shelters to continue twisting cordage from plant fibers. Others cook foraged plants or work leather while steam rises from damp clothing. A few wander into the drizzle to gather more wood before returning to the warmth of the flames. Among them is historical craft specialist and YouTube educator Vasi Birchwood . For Birchwood, weather isn't an inconvenience so much as another participant in this meeting of experiential archeologists and craft experts in Northern Germany. That shift in perspective is just one of the many ways she does more than dress like a Neolithic person at these gatherings. pages.text: The Astronomical Problem of Space Junk Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images by Samantha Lawler / NASA / smspsy via Adobe Stock and public domain We have launched all manner of satellite and machinery into low-Earth orbit. But what goes up must come down. Most often, these items burn up in the atmosphere upon re-entry, which isn’t good for air quality or the ozone layer. But not everything incinerates — and increasing amounts of debris are hurtling back toward Earth and landing in backyards and farm fields. Falling detritus disrupts air travel and risks collision with infrastructure and people on the ground. There are those who argue that additional regulation is required around the launching and de-orbiting of these materials. In this episode, host Ari Daniel speaks with astronomer Samantha Lawler and Smithsonian contributing writer Dan Falk about space junk and the concern among researchers that it is becoming a growing threat to public safety. The continent of North America has been inhabited by humans for at least 16,500 years. As early as the 1500s, early settlers and European thinkers were interested in discovering how humans had come to populate North and South America. One theory suggested the migration of Norsemen across Greenland into North America. Another theory proposed the island of Atlantis as the origins of human life in the New World. Yet another idea proposed that the inhabitants had generated out of mud. However, by the early 1800s, scientists and theorists began discussing the possibility of a land bridge that had spanned between Asia and North America thousands of years ago. Stephen Power, Alamy By Natasha Colyer Published September 17, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The allure of the skies is nothing new. For all of human history people have looked up to the inky blackness of night and marvelled at the stars. Yet true darkness just isn’t something Europeans experience in the same way anymore due to artificial light illuminating the night sky. Light pollution can disrupt sleep and circadian rhythms, affect wildlife and ecosystems, and contribute to unnecessary energy use and carbon emissions. With this in mind, it’s no surprise more of us than ever are swapping chasing the sun for chasing the stars instead. DarkSky International is a non-profit organisation that certifies destinations around the world for the quality of their night skies, their approach to artificial lighting, conservation efforts and long-term commitment to protecting darkness. pages.text: The Best Ski Areas in Austria This Season | National Geographic TRAVEL Where to Ski in Austria This Season Austria’s mix of beginner slopes, black runs and mountainside culture works for all — from fun-seeking families to hardcore off-pisters. From expertly maintained beginners’ pistes to some of the highest slopes in the Alps, Austria offers a wide range of ski resorts for travellers. Pawel Kazmierczak, Alamy Stock Photo By Mike MacEacheran Last updated November 10, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Traditionally, Europe’s best all-rounder, Austria looks set to give France a run for its money this season as the favourite destination — certainly among British skiers who love its reliably beautiful pistes and oodles of old-school Alpine charm. Austria’s sky-scraping corner of the Alps has a diverse offering. It’s home to some of the region’s highest peaks and most challenging slopes, along with expertly maintained beginners’ pistes and family-friendly hamlets set in postcard-perfect mountain villages where winter sports have been woven into local culture for centuries. Whether you’re skiing, partying or enjoying one of Austria’s many mountain festivals, those with summit gleams in their eyes can easily experience a winter break where serious powder highs and oompah-pop-fuelled apres is the norm. pages.text: The Best Ski Resorts in Japan This Season | National Geographic TRAVEL The Best Ski Resorts in Japan This Season With its abundant deep snow and unique apres-ski, Japan is attracting an increasing number of skiers from overseas. Get the inside guide, from resorts to ramen. Silver birch trees flank the slopes in Niseko Grand Hirafu ski resort in Hokkaido. Anthony Brown, Alamy By Tristan Kennedy Published November 8, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Renowned for its distinctive skiing culture, Japan is the ultimate wish list destination for serious skiers and snowboarders. If you’re used to the slopes of Europe or North America, you’ll appreciate the small differences: in the menu at a mountain cafe, the particular etiquette of the onsen, or even the heated toilet seats; everything feels different in Japan. But the main claim to fame is its soft, lightweight and very consistent powder snow. Westerly winds whip off the Siberian tundra and scoop up moisture over the Sea of Japan, before dumping it as snow over the archipelago. This quirk of geography means that parts of the northern island of Hokkaido are blessed with up to 15 metres of snowfall every winter compared to, say, seven metres in European resorts such as Tignes, France. Replenished near-daily, fluffy Japanese snow is incredibly forgiving for skiers and boarders, earning it a special nickname among aficionados: ‘Ja-pow’. pages.text: The best sources of protein for a balanced diet | National Geographic SCIENCE These are the best ways to get your protein Protein helps you build muscle and even powers the immune system. But it’s not always easy to get enough, especially if you follow a plant-based diet. Protein is an essential building block for life and a staple of our diet. However, not all sources of protein are equally beneficial to our health. Photograph by fcafotodigital, Getty Images By Joel Mathis Published September 13, 2024 Protein is a really important component of a proper diet. You might be familiar with the role it plays in helping you build muscle and feeling full after a meal—but that’s not all it can do. “Protein plays a crucial role to our physiology,” says Jessica Corwin, lead registered dietician at Corewell Health, a hospital group in Michigan. Protein-rich foods provide amino acids that the body uses to build and repair tissues, power the immune system, and even help regulate hormones. The recommended daily allowance is based on your body weight: About 0.36 grams for every pound that you weigh. That’s about 54 grams of protein a day for a 150-pound person. ( How much protein do you really need ?) But it’s not always easy to get enough protein—especially if you’re trying to follow a plant-based diet. pages.text: The best summers of my life were spent at the Grand Canyon Lodge. Now it’s gone. | National Geographic By Leath Tonino Published July 18, 2025 I’m not usually one to get weepy over a hotel, let alone a patio and some rough-hewn wooden furniture. But when Arizona’s famous Grand Canyon Lodge and a number of smaller adjacent structures burned down on the night of July 12 in the Dragon Bravo Fire, a blaze that to date has consumed 11,344 acres and remains entirely uncontained, it left a hole in more than just the conifer forest of the North Rim . My heart, my friends’ hearts—there’s a hole in each of these now. And there are similar holes in the hearts of thousands of folks across the globe who also loved, and still love, and will forever love, that rustic palace, that gobsmacking view, that superlative place. ( Grand Canyon National Park Photos) In 2024, close to five million visitors experienced the beauty and wonder of Grand Canyon National Park , but only ten percent of them ventured to the high, green, thrillingly remote North Rim. For those that did make the five-hour drive from Las Vegas, or the six-hour drive from Flagstaff, or the seven-hour drive from Salt Lake City, the Grand Canyon Lodge, which until this past weekend perched at an elevation of 8,000 feet near the tip of Bright Angel Point, was invariably the destination. pages.text: The Best Way to See the Nile? Take a Slow Cruise Aboard a Dahabiya | National Geographic TRAVEL The Best Way to See the Nile? Take a Slow Cruise Aboard a Dahabiya Travelling aboard a traditional dahabiya reveals the slow side of life on the Nile — one where fisherfolk ply the waters and families invite guests into their kitchens. Dahabiya cruises are among the most intimate and comfortable journeys down the Nile. Claire Thomas By Zoey Goto Published September 1, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). A sharp crack echoes across the Nile. Then another. Barefoot in a green-and-white tin boat scarcely wider than his shoulders, fisherman Fahmy Hassan brings a wooden pole crashing down onto the water. Each strike sends spray flying, inadvertently flushing an indignant yellow-footed egret from the reeds. Earlier that morning, before my group boarded the dinky boats south of Edfu to watch the fishermen of Bisaw Island at work, Fahmy had explained the age-old technique: striking the water sends vibrations rippling through the river, driving fish towards his waiting net. Curious to see if it works, we watch as he begins hauling the net in, hand over hand. For a moment, it looks empty. Then a silver-grey catfish glints beneath the mesh, prompting cheers from both the fishermen and visitors. “This is nothing,” he says with a laugh, holding up the wriggling catch between pinched fingers. pages.text: The Big Rail Fare Freeze | National Rail Skip to main content The Big Rail Fare Freeze Rail fares have been frozen for the first time in 30 years, and passengers are expected to save around £600 million this year, making rail more affordable and helping to ease cost-of-living pressures. The fares freeze means that regulated train tickets (the ones where pricing is set by government and not train companies) have been frozen across England until March 2027. This includes Standard class Season Tickets , Anytime tickets and Off-Peak tickets but doesn’t automatically cover journeys that are entirely in Scotland or Wales. First Class and Standard Premium tickets are not included, along with Transport for Wales, Caledonian Sleeper and TfL services. They are the responsibility of devolved nations or regional authorities. Hull Trains, Lumo, Grand Central, and Heathrow Express are also not included as they are independent operations without a government contract. They choose their own routes and set their own fares. If you’re unsure about your route, please contact your train company , who will be able to confirm. Changes to fares resulting from the fares reform (e.g. the introduction of pay as you go (PAYG)) may result in ticket types, products and/or time restrictions being altered. Find out more in the government announcement . A similar scheme exists for ScotRail in Scotland and for Merseyrail . FAQs How is the fares freeze benefitting customers? By Nicholas St. Fleur Published March 30, 2026 A newly discovered Spinosaurus sporting a bizarre, curved blade-like crest has snatched the headlines. New medicines are now preventing most dangerous bleeds, while gene therapy may offer some patients years of protection after a single treatment. As young children, Kapono, now 18, and Duke, 13, bruised frequently. “They’d be black and blue down their shins, on their forearms, and even on their faces after bumping into things,” Pavao recalls. Kapono also kickboxes and previously played baseball and skateboarded—activities that would have been unthinkable for many children with hemophilia just a few decades ago. By Mark Hay Published February 27, 2026 As a matter of pragmatism and genuine preference, cultures across the globe have long and storied histories of cooking with offal—a catch-all term for every part of an animal that isn’t a slab of muscle meat. Yet for all that history, over the last few decades, offal consumption has declined worldwide, says food scientist Carlos Álvarez, especially in developed countries like the United States. As the “mild” flavor (compared to other parts of the animal) and sanitized packaging of factory farmed muscle becomes the norm, explains Amy Bentley, a professor of food studies at New York University, eaters find the distinctive form, flavors, and textures of recognizable brains, tangy livers, and mushy glands increasing unnerving . But the disappearance of offal from modern foodways plays a part in food waste. Reports vary based on what their authors consider edible offal versus inedible items (some exclude bone, although much of it is edible), and which animal they examine. The crown’s harsh laws had backfired, reminding colonists that they were at the mercy of the whims of King George and his Parliament. Twelve of the Colonies sent delegates to Carpenters’ Hall, a brick building in central Philadelphia. Georgia declined to participate, wary of alienating the British as it faced threats from nearby Native American nations. East Florida and West Florida, then in the hands of the British, also did not participate. The First Continental Congress convened at Carpenters’ Hall in Philadelphia—a setting associated with common Americans—in September 1774 to debate how to respond to the Intolerable Acts that placed Massachusetts under military rule. Before the discovery of “Sue,” “Stan,” “Scotty,” and many other famous skeletons of Earth’s last great carnivorous dinosaur, AMNH 5027 was the icon. pages.text: The deadly race to decipher Maya hieroglyphs | National Geographic By George E. Stuart Photographs by Otis Imboden Published March 6, 2026 This story originally published in the December 1975 issue of National Geographic magazine. See more digitized stories from our archives here . Murder and Maya hieroglyphs make an unlikely combination, but the two came together one evening several years ago, deep in the rain forest of northern Guatemala. It happened at La Naya, soon after Scotsman Ian Graham and his party had arrived to draw and photograph inscriptions that had been reported at the remote ruin. They found much more than they bargained for. "I never thought Maya archeology would be that dangerous," Ian told me when I visited him at Harvard University's Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, "but I sometimes feel fortunate to be alive. The looters are quite serious about their business." At La Naya, Ian and his group had unwittingly interrupted a gang of men engaged in cutting apart an ancient stone monument. SCIENCE LAELAPS The Echoes of Toothed Birds By Riley Black Published May 22, 2015 • 4 min read Whenever I spot a grebe, I try to imagine the bird with teeth. This is another symptom of a chronically fossiliferous mind. You see, these snake-necked swimming birds have traditionally been taken as a proxy for a specific sort of ancient avian called hesperornithiforms. Best known by, as you might guess, Hesperornis – these toothed birds pioneered the diving lifestyle between 113 and 66 million years ago. Today’s grebes and loons look like edentulous echos of these lost Cretaceous days, or, as beautifully expressed by ornithologist William Beebe : When in the depth of the winter, a full hundred miles from the nearest land, one sees a loon in the path of the steamer, listens to its weird, maniacal laughter, and sees it slowly sink downward through the green waters, it truly seems a hint of the bird-life of long-past ages. No surprise, then, that paleontologists past sometimes considered loons and grebes to be the descendants of Hesperornis . Their bones carry the same superficial similarity. But this is an evolutionary ruse known as convergence. Loons and grebes are copycats that independently took up the same lifestyle as the toothed birds that dove after fish in warm Cretaceous seas and sometimes wound up in the stomachs of monstrous marine reptiles. How Scientists Are Making Medicine Needle-Free From insulin inhalers to epinephrine nasal sprays, new delivery systems are making some lifesaving drugs easier to take. From nasal sprays to inhaled drugs, new technologies are making it possible for some medicines to reach the bloodstream without a needle. Rebecca Hale, National Geographic By Meryl Davids Landau Published September 28, 2026 For decades, treating a life-threatening allergic reaction outside a hospital meant reaching for an epinephrine auto-injector. Now, some patients can reach for a nasal spray instead. That new option, along with other injection-free medicines that have recently become available, could be especially consequential for people who fear needles. Nearly all young children and many teens and adults recoil at getting a shot—with some so paralyzed they avoid needed treatments and vaccines. That hesitation can have serious health consequences. When a child has a severe allergic reaction, for example, some caregivers avoid emergency epinephrine auto-injectors because they fear hurting the child or the child is nervous about the prick. Delaying the medicine during anaphylaxis may cause serious symptoms to reappear hours later and lead to significantly longer ER stays. pages.text: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe' Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe' 6 November 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Chris Baraniuk Technology reporter Rolls-Royce A jet engine will have hundreds of turbine blades Every time you fly, an extraordinary feat of endurance occurs inside the aircraft's engines. Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C. It is a true engineering marvel. And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown. During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours. A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification. Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes. "It's about as complicated as manufacturing gets," says Ben Fifoot, manufacturing engineer at Rolls-Royce, which makes turbine blades in the UK. "It's a real motivator to get out of bed in the morning." There may be no better illustration of the critical and integral role the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has played in the history of our nation’s health than the timely juxtaposition of two anniversaries occurring this year – our nation’s 250th and the FDA’s 120th. That’s because this confluence underscores how, for nearly half of our nation’s existence, Americans have relied on, and benefited from, the FDA’s oversight of our food, medical products, veterinary products, cosmetics, and so much more. The FDA’s regulatory role began in 1906 with the passage of the Pure Food and Drugs Act, which authorized the Bureau of Chemistry—the FDA’s immediate predecessor—to regulate contaminated, misbranded, and dangerous foods and medicines. The agency did not receive its present name, the Food and Drug Administration, until 1930. Over time, the FDA’s basic law has been repeatedly amended, augmented, and strengthened in response to gaps or shortcomings, further enhancing the FDA’s essential role as the nation’s guardian of public health. pages.text: The federal budget process | USAGov Skip to main content The federal budget process Learn about the federal government’s budget process. Steps include the president creating the budget plan and Congress’s work creating funding bills for the president to sign. Annual funding areas Every year, the U.S. Congress begins work on a federal budget for the next fiscal year. The federal government’s fiscal year runs from October 1 of one calendar year through September 30 of the next. And the annual budget covers three spending areas: Mandatory spending - funding for Social Security, Medicare, veterans benefits, and other spending required by law. This typically uses over half of all funding. Discretionary spending - federal agency funding. Congress sets funding levels for these each year. This usually accounts for around a third of all funding. Interest on the debt - this usually uses less than 10 percent of all funding. Creating the U.S. federal budget The budget planning begins a year before the budget is to go into effect. Federal agencies create budget requests and submit them to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB). OMB refers to the agencies’ requests as it develops the budget proposal for the president. The president submits the budget proposal to Congress early the next year. Proposed funding is divided among 12 subcommittees, which hold hearings. Each handles funding for different government functions such as defense spending or energy and water. P. Cartier/Bridgeman/ACI By Javier Negrete Published February 15, 2024 The Roman Republic was booming in the beginning of the fourth century B.C. Wealthy and powerful, it had just defeated the Etruscan city of Veii, amassed an immense war chest, and doubled its territory. But then, out of the blue, the republic suffered the unthinkable: occupation by a Celtic people, the Gauls. This was the first time that Rome and Gaul would face off, but it would not be the last. Over the coming centuries, the Romans and the Gauls would clash many times. But this first defeat in 387 B.C. caused a collective trauma for Rome that lasted generations, shaping Roman attitudes toward all peoples from the north. ( How was Rome founded? Not in a day, and not by twins. ) Early encounters By 600 B.C. the Gallic people Insubres had already settled south of the Alps, where they founded Mediolanum (today’s Milan). Over the next two centuries, other Gallic peoples would do the same and expand into southern and western Europe. An inflatable vest that helps divers control their depth, this buoyancy compensator belonged to ocean scientist Sylvia Earle before becoming a part of National Geographic’s collection. Rebecca Hale, NGM Staff By Rachel Slade Published October 15, 2026 Oceanographer and marine biologist Sylvia Earle wore this sea-beaten vest in the mid-1970s, designed to help divers rise, sink, or hover by adding or releasing air. Earle, now 91 and both a National Geographic Explorer at Large and Rolex Testimonee , led the first all-woman aquanaut research team in 1970 and later served as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s first female chief scientist, among many other achievements. The vest is one of several pieces of gear in the archives that once belonged to “Her Deepness”—the nickname Earle picked up after setting a still-unbeaten record, in 1979, for the deepest untethered walk on the ocean floor. Other items in the collection include a pair of diving fins that Earle wore during a 1991 trip to the oil-slicked waters of the Persian Gulf. pages.text: The Global Web of Subsea Cables That Connects the World Can Now Detect Whales—Even When They're Silent Skip to main content A blue whale has been gathering food deep within the water column and reaches the surface with its throat pleats still distended, forming an enormous pouch. Within a few moments the whale will right itself up, expell the water, swallow the food, take several breaths and dive again. Francois Gohier/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Nearly 1,000 feet below the sea off the coast of Norway’s Svalbard archipelago, on a glass cable the width of a human hair, scientists detect a massive object moving through the water. It’s so big that the water it displaces when it moves produces low-frequency waves that radiate outward from its body. These waves ripple away toward the seafloor, where they stretch the tiny glass cable, buried beneath the seabed, almost imperceptibly. Onshore, laser pulses are fired down the cable, and as the light travels, microscopic imperfections scatter the light in the glass. Often, when researchers get feedback like this, it’s a submarine moving over the cable, or even a large ship chugging along the surface above. But today, they’ve found a blue whale. Typically, to find whales, scientists use a hydrophone, essentially an underwater microphone that can pick up a whale’s calls. They’re often fixed to the seabed or suspended from research vessels. pages.text: The greatest library in the world was built by this ruthless king | National Geographic By Michela Piccin Published January 21, 2026 Ashurbanipal, the most powerful king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire in the mid-seventh century B.C., was known for his ruthless military prowess, his incredible lion-hunting skills—and for being a librarian. “Palace of Ashurbanipal, King of the Universe, King of Assyria” reads an inscription denoting his ownership on one of over 30,000 clay tablets and fragments from the magnificent library he maintained at his capital, Nineveh, today in northern Iraq. The 19th-century discovery of the library by British archaeologists was a game changer for Assyrian studies. Previously, documented sources on Ashurbanipal consisted of one reference in the Bible and often fanciful accounts of his life in later classical texts. With the discovery of the tablets—on which scribes had used reeds to impress cuneiform (wedge-shaped) letters—the beliefs, liturgy, medicine, politics, and diplomacy of the Assyrian world came into sharp focus. Among the many tablets brought to London was a fragment of the earliest long-form literary work ever found: the Epic of Gilgamesh. Containing stories such as that of the Great Flood, also found in the Bible, the epic electrified 19th-century scholarship. Seeking Nineveh Nineteenth-century British scholars had a fascination with the region of Mesopotamia, inspired by their interest in cities named in the Bible. pages.text: The Guardian SecureDrop The Guardian SecureDrop Share stories with us securely and confidentially SecureDrop is a tool to help people securely send messages and documents to the Guardian. It uses the Tor network to preserve source anonymity by hiding where messages came from. All communication is encrypted in transit and on our server. To avoid surveillance and interception, submissions from sources are decrypted on a device that is isolated from both the internet and our internal networks. To access our SecureDrop site you need to use a browser application that can access the Tor network . Use of the Tor network helps hide your identity online, but it does not guarantee the safety of the computer that you use to contact us. We recommend that you avoid accessing SecureDrop from small networks where use of a Tor browser may be monitored or restricted. If there is any risk of your browser activity being recorded, it's advisable not to jump straight from this information page to the actual Guardian SecureDrop site. You could instead make a note of the SecureDrop ‘onion’ URL (see below) and then wait to connect to that site at another time or on a different computer. The other half are trillions of microbes that thrive on or inside your body to form a group of biological communities known as the human microbiome. These microbial communities can vary greatly in size and character. The digestive tract hosts the largest number of microbes, forming a complex ecosystem known as the gut microbiome. Concentrated primarily in the large intestine, it consists of thousands of different species of bacteria, viruses, fungi and other microorganisms . Like a fingerprint, your gut microbiome is entirely unique. It starts developing the moment you are born. Over time, the amount and types of microorganisms change based on factors such as your environment and diet. Why is the gut microbiome important? The back of an archival glass-plate transparency shows the State of Liberty in reverse (Lady Liberty actually holds her torch in her right hand). Getting this shot in 1930 required a feat of technical imagination. MELVILLE BELL GROSVENOR, NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC IMAGE COLLECTION By Rachel Slade Published August 11, 2026 Some of the earliest aerial photos ever taken in color were committed to gelatin-coated glass plates now held in the National Geographic archives . They include this sweeping shot of the Statue of Liberty , shown here on the back of an old plate rimmed with fraying labels. The scene was captured in 1930 by National Geographic magazine Assistant Editor (and future Editor in Chief) Melville Bell Grosvenor—a photo it would have been all but impossible to make without a bit of ingenuity and two groundbreaking technologies. The first was known as the Finlay color process, a photography technique that exposed a glass-plate negative through a screen of colored filters. Unlike the color photo methods that came before, the Finlay process didn’t require long exposures and absolute stillness, which were impossible to achieve while cruising through the air, particularly aboard the jostling prop planes that then dominated the skies.
